paras: The attempted lynching of John Glenn took place at Sandy Hill, Washington County, New York, on November 7, 1888, when a crowd tried to seize Glenn, a baseball player accused of assaulting a nine-year-old girl, from the policemen who had arrested him. In the struggle a policeman's revolver went off and the ball struck Glenn in the neck; most reports called the shooting accidental, while one wire brief said a member of the mob fired. A Vermont paper reported a week later that Glenn had died.

Glenn was described as a former baseball player who had lived in Rochester and played there with the "old Alerts." A Connecticut sports column identified him as the left fielder of the old Chicago League club in 1873 and 1874. The New York Sun repeated hearsay that he had served a western prison term for assaulting a woman and had assaulted his niece.

According to a Glens Falls dispatch in the Sun, at about two o'clock two nine-year-old girls, Helen Sherrill and Nellie Lloyd, went to an outbuilding behind the Union school, where Glenn offered them candy. The dispatch said he seized and assaulted Helen Sherrill, who broke free and ran screaming from the yard. Her cries drew a crowd that chased Glenn; Policeman Gilson Mason caught him, but he broke away and hid in the cellar of M. G. Paris's house, where Policeman Morrison found him.

Glenn was driven in a cart to the office of Police Justice Sullivan, where, the Sun said, several hundred men armed with clubs had gathered and made "arrangements" to lynch him. When the cart reached the sidewalk the crowd rushed the prisoner and landed blows on him while Morrison held them back with his revolver. In a second rush someone jerked the policeman's arm, the revolver went off, and the ball entered Glenn's neck below the right jaw and lodged in his brain. The western wire version said the officer had drawn the pistol to force a passage and the crowd "forced his hand up." Glenn was carried, still alive, to his brother's house, and the Sun reported that the girl would recover.

That evening, the Sun reported, many prominent citizens called on Morrison at his house and absolved him of all blame. The same dispatch said that if Glenn had not been shot the mob would have hanged him from the nearest lamp post, and it predicted that if he survived he would "most assuredly be lynched." On November 16 the Essex County Herald of Guildhall, Vermont, reported that Glenn, "accidentally shot by the policeman who was protecting him from the mob," had died "in great agony." No report of an inquest or of arrests among the crowd appears in the coverage.

The Sun ran the fullest account on November 8 under the headline "Sandy Hill Up in Arms," with decks announcing that a crowd had tried "to lynch the culprit" and that a policeman had accidentally shot his prisoner. The same day the Camden Evening Telegram printed a one-sentence Glens Falls item, "Prisoner Shot," stating that Glenn was "fatally shot by one of a mob which wanted to lynch him."

A different wire version ran in western papers on November 9, from Sacramento and Seattle to Salt Lake City, Los Angeles and Unionville, Nevada. Their headlines treated the charge as settled: "Fate of a Brute," "A Rapist Shot," "A Fiend Fatally Wounded," and, in Seattle, "John Glenn, the Lecherous Baseball Player, in New Trouble." The Los Angeles paper headed the same text "A Fallen Baseballist," and a week later a Waterbury, Connecticut, sports column treated the shooting as baseball news. None of the reports gave Glenn's race.

Accounts differed on who fired the shot: the Sun, the western wire and the Essex County Herald attributed it to the policeman's revolver going off when the crowd jerked or forced his arm, while the Camden brief said "one of a mob" shot him. Early reports of the wound ranged from "probably a fatal wound" to "fatally shot," while the Sun had him still alive. The Waterbury column placed the shooting "near Rochester," Glenn's former home, rather than at Sandy Hill.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of John Glenn
bases: A crowd tried to take an arrested man accused of assaulting a child from the police to hang him, and he was shot in the struggle (A1, A2, A3).

A crowd of several hundred tried to seize and hang Glenn over an assault charge, and a later brief reports that he died (A1, A9); but the fullest account and two others say the fatal shot came from the protecting policeman's revolver, discharged accidentally when the crowd jerked his arm, and only one brief says a mob member shot him (A1, A3, A9 against A2), so the mob's attempt is best treated as an attempted lynching.
The New York Sun's dispatch and the separate western wire agree on the arrest, the crowd and the neck wound (A1, A3), though Glenn's death rests on a single later brief (A9).

accounts.label: Glens Falls dispatch (New York Sun)
accounts.gist: Someone in the crowd jerked Policeman Morrison's arm during a rush and his revolver went off, hitting Glenn; the headline calls the shooting accidental and says the mob would otherwise have hanged him.

accounts.label: Western wire
accounts.gist: The officer drew his pistol to force a passage, the crowd forced his hand up, and the discharge gave Glenn a probably fatal neck wound.

accounts.label: Camden wire brief
accounts.gist: Glenn, in an officer's custody, was fatally shot by one of a mob that wanted to lynch him.

accounts.label: Vermont news brief
accounts.gist: Glenn, accidentally shot by the policeman protecting him from the mob, died in great agony.

framing.detail: The Sun's 'Sandy Hill Up in Arms' told the lynching attempt in detail, reported citizens absolving the policeman and predicted Glenn would 'most assuredly be lynched' if he lived, without comment on the mob.
Western reprints headlined Glenn as 'a Brute', 'A Rapist', 'A Fiend' and 'the Lecherous Baseball Player', treating the accusation as fact.
The Camden paper ran a one-line 'Prisoner Shot' brief saying a mob member fired.

conflicts.note: The Sun's detailed dispatch, the western wire and the later Vermont brief agree on the officer's revolver; the Camden version is a single sentence.

conflicts.note: The earlier reports were written the day after the shooting; the death report, published a week later, is the latest word but stands alone.
Rochester was Glenn's former residence according to the Sun; the sports column appears to have confused the two.
